title: A coin in a fish (Matthew 17:14–27)
hook: free, and paying anyway: a tax, a fish, and faith the size of a seed
tomorrow: the disciples ask who's the greatest. why does he call over a child?

segments.voice: Yesterday’s word was tell no one: a vision kept quiet, and a hand on three frightened friends. Now they walk back down the mountain, into a crowd.
screen: `ARISE, BE NOT AFRAID.` → `BACK DOWN THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Anyone who has paid a fee they were pretty sure they didn't owe, just to stop an argument, will recognize this scene. In Capernaum, the men who collect the temple tax stop Peter: "Doth not your master pay tribute?" Peter says yes, fast, the way you answer at a door. Inside, Jesus asks him a question. Kings collect from strangers, or from their own children? Strangers, Peter says. "Then are the children free." So Jesus doesn't owe it. And he pays anyway. With a coin from a fish's mouth. Why?
screen: `A FEE YOU DON'T OWE.` → `THEN ARE THE CHILDREN FREE.` → `AND HE PAYS ANYWAY?`

segments.voice: Start with his reason, which Matthew gives in four words: "lest we should offend them." He's free, and he pays, so that nobody stumbles over a small thing. Then the odd part. Go to the sea, he tells Peter, cast a hook, take the first fish that comes up, open its mouth, and you'll find a piece of money. "That take, and give unto them for me and thee." He sends a fisherman to do the one thing he already knows how to do. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: Matthew never says Peter caught the fish. The chapter ends on the instruction. Earlier that same chapter, the disciples had failed to heal a boy and asked why. Jesus answered, because of your unbelief, and then: "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." So that's the puzzle solved. Not a mountain of faith. A seed of it. One coin, one cast line, one small trust, enough to cover a debt for two. The big things in this chapter keep turning out small.
screen: `LEST WE SHOULD OFFEND THEM.` · `CAST A HOOK, OPEN ITS MOUTH.` · `MATTHEW NEVER SHOWS THE CATCH.` · `FAITH AS A GRAIN OF MUSTARD SEED.` · then, large: `FAITH MOVES MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you owe: a few dollars, a borrowed book, a thank-you you never sent. If you can settle it from where you're sitting, do it now, quickly and without a fuss; if not, decide exactly when. Small is enough here. That was the whole point of the seed.
A coin in a fish. A tax Jesus didn't owe, paid anyway, from the first fish on Peter's hook.
screen: `A COIN IN A FISH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Hold onto this one: faith moves mountains, and it starts the size of a seed. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1458 COUNTS.` → `MATTHEW, READ THROUGH · 32 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DOES HE CALL OVER A CHILD?`

howItsDone: Christians often quote the mustard seed line when someone feels their faith is too small, and some read Matthew 17 as a picture of paying what's asked even when you could argue it.

fork.setup: your friend says you owe four dollars for snacks. you're fairly sure you don't, and she's getting annoyed. what does the fish story point toward?
options: pay it, without a fuss, so a small thing doesn't become a big one.
prove you're right first; Jesus said the children are free.
pay it, but tell everyone you never actually owed it.
fork.reveal: Jesus says the children are free, and pays anyway, lest we should offend them. being right and paying aren't opposites.

chat.meaning: Faith as a grain of mustard seed is enough to move a mountain, Jesus says. The size he names is tiny on purpose.

notes: 'The temple tax': the KJV says 'tribute'; the Greek didrachma is usually understood as the temple tax (cf. Exodus 30:13). Confirm the gloss and the voice's 'temple tax'.
'Matthew gives in four words': 'lest we should offend them' is four words in the KJV. 'Because of your unbelief' (17:20) is quoted closely without quotation marks.
Puzzle shape: the chapter's order is the healing and the mustard seed (17:14–21) before the tax (17:24–27); the voice says 'earlier that same chapter' to keep the order honest.
Practice kind: one small act (settling a small debt), from the outline's 'pay a small debt cheerfully'.
